capitulo.titulo: 1.2 Types of business entities: who owns it, who pays

visual.titulo: Unit 1 poster: 1.2 Types of business entities
visual.pie: Private vs public sectors, sole traders, partnerships, companies, cooperatives, NGOs

turnos.t: Welcome to part two: unit one point two, types of business entities.
Here is the box from your class poster.
Private versus public sectors, sole traders, partnerships, private and public companies, cooperatives, and non-governmental organizations.
Behind all of them sits one simple question.
Who owns the business, and who pays if it goes wrong?
If your business fails, could you lose your flat?
It depends on the legal form you chose.
So let's start with ownership.
The private sector is owned and controlled by private individuals or groups, and it usually aims for profit.
The public sector is owned and controlled by the government, and it usually provides essential services, funded mainly by taxes.

visual.pie: Renfe AVE at Barcelona Sants: owned by the Spanish state, so public sector

turnos.t: This train belongs to Renfe, Spain's state railway operator, so it is in the public sector.
Why would a government run a business at all?
First, to provide services the private sector might under-supply, like trains to rural areas, which a profit-seeking firm could close.
Second, to control strategic industries, like a national electricity grid.
Third, to keep prices affordable for everyone.
Critics reply that state firms can be less efficient without the profit motive.
A typical four-mark question: distinguish between the private sector and the public sector.
Define each by ownership, one mark each.
Then compare the aim, with an example of each: a family bike shop that aims for profit, and Renfe, which provides a public service.

visual.nota: Unlimited liability: personal assets can be taken to pay business debts

pasos.detalle: Investors only lose what they put in
More people are willing to buy shares
It can grow faster than a sole trader

turnos.t: The key idea of this unit is liability: responsibility for debts.
Unlimited liability means the owners are personally responsible for all the debts of the business, so they may have to use personal assets, even their home, to pay them.
Limited liability means shareholders can only lose the money they invested.
Their personal assets are protected. Why?
Because a company is a separate legal entity.
It can own assets, sign contracts, sue and be sued in its own name.
This is incorporation.
Now follow the chain.
Investors only risk what they put in, so more people buy shares, the company raises more capital, and it can grow faster.

puntos: Easy and cheap to set up
No continuity if the owner dies

turnos.t: The first for-profit form is the sole trader: an individual who owns and runs a business alone.
Think of a freelancer, a tailor or a restaurant owner.
They can employ staff, but the staff own nothing.
The advantages: it is easy and cheap to set up, the owner keeps all the profit, decides quickly, offers a personal service, and the accounts stay private.
The disadvantages: unlimited liability, finance limited to savings and loans, a heavy workload, a high risk of failure against bigger rivals, and no continuity.
There is little legal distinction between owner and business, so if the owner dies, the business usually stops.
Even Chanel started this way, with Coco Chanel, in nineteen ten.

filas: What if a partner leaves or dies

turnos.t: A partnership is owned by two or more partners, who share capital, skills, workload and profit.
Doctors' practices and law firms are classic examples.
Write two or more partners: the old rule of two to twenty is not in your syllabus.
Partners normally sign a partnership deed, a contract covering the points on screen.
Advantages: easy to set up, more finance than one person, partners specialise, and accounts stay private.
Disadvantages: partners usually have unlimited liability, and each can be responsible for decisions made by the others.
Decisions are slower, and disagreements are the classic risk.
Some countries also allow limited partnerships, where sleeping partners have limited liability.

visual.pie: Mercadona: very large, but privately held. Its shares are not on a stock exchange

turnos.t: Now companies.
A company is owned by shareholders, who vote at the annual general meeting and elect the board of directors.
They may receive a dividend, a share of profit, but dividends are not guaranteed: profit can be reinvested.

To form a company, owners file a memorandum of association, with basic details like the name and share capital, and articles of association, the internal rules on directors, voting and shareholders' rights.
In a privately held company, shares are sold privately to people the owners choose, and are not traded on a stock exchange.
Mercadona and Mars are huge examples, so size does not define the type.
Advantages: limited liability, control over who joins, and privacy for a long-term view.
Disadvantages: less capital, and shares are hard to sell.

escenas.titulo: Publicly held companies and the IPO

turnos.t: A publicly held company has its shares traded on a stock exchange, so anyone can buy them.
A privately held company goes public through an initial public offering: the first sale of its shares to the public.
Inditex has been listed in Madrid since two thousand and one.
The advantage is capital: share sales raise huge sums, and risk is spread among many shareholders.
The costs: an expensive set-up, published accounts, profits shared among many, and loss of control, because a rival can buy enough shares to take over.
Also, thousands of shareholders own it, but professional managers run it, and they may chase their own goals.
That is the divorce of ownership and control.
And remember: publicly held does not mean owned by the government.

tarjetas.detalle: Sell in markets with a social aim: Aravind Eye Care
Provide public services, e.g. recycling or ambulances
Owned and run by members: Mondragon
All surplus back into the mission: Red Cross

turnos.t: A social enterprise trades to achieve a social or environmental purpose, and reinvests most of its surplus in that purpose.
The term describes its purpose, not its legal form.
For-profit social enterprises make a profit but build impact into the business model.
The syllabus lists three types.
Private sector companies, like Aravind Eye Care in India, with affordable cataract surgery.
Public sector companies, providing services usually supplied by the state, such as recycling or ambulances under government contracts. And cooperatives.
Then come non-profit social enterprises, such as non-governmental organizations.
For Paper three, know their challenges: patient funding, credibility and greenwashing accusations, measuring impact, complex supply chains, and staying true to the purpose as they grow.

visual.pie: Mondragon Corporation headquarters (Gipuzkoa): a group of worker cooperatives

turnos.t: This is the headquarters of Mondragon, in the Basque Country, a group of cooperatives owned by their worker-members.
A cooperative is a business owned and run by its members, such as workers, customers or producers, who share the decision-making and the surplus.
Two features for a four-mark question.
One: members own it, so the surplus is shared among them or reinvested, not paid to outside shareholders.
Two: democratic control, usually one member, one vote, whatever they invested.
The weakness: decisions can be slow, and raising capital is harder.
Your notes add the argan oil cooperatives of Berber women in Morocco.
Selling together, they negotiate directly with international buyers, and get salaries, health insurance, childcare and literacy classes.

visual.pie: Spanish Red Cross volunteers: an NGO, a non-profit social enterprise

turnos.t: Red Cross is a non-governmental organization: a non-profit social enterprise, independent of government, that pursues a social or environmental mission and reinvests any surplus in it.
Oxfam Intermón and Amnesty International are others. Two traps.
Non-profit does not mean unpaid: these organizations can employ paid staff and make a surplus, but the surplus goes back into the mission.
And independent does not mean no public money: they can receive government grants.
They are financed by donations, grants, membership fees and trading, like charity shops.
Advantages: no tax on reinvested surplus, and volunteers keep costs low.
The big weakness is unstable funding.
Donations fall in a recession, so many build trading arms to steady their income.

visual.nota: No single best form: match it to the case

turnos.t: Recommend questions ask you to match the entity to the situation: the aim, the capital needed, the risk, and the control the owner wants.
Take Luis, a sole trader with a bike shop in Barcelona.
He made forty-eight thousand euros profit and wants a second shop costing sixty thousand.
His friend Ana, a mechanic, offers thirty thousand.
Luis has a mortgage on his flat, and wants the final say on style.
A partnership brings Ana's money and skills, but unlimited liability puts his flat at risk.
A privately held company protects the flat, and if Luis keeps a majority of the shares, he keeps control.
So recommend the company, with conditions: for example, Luis holds fifty-five percent.
